title: 2 Simple Strategies To Improve Listening
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin presents two quick, sequential strategies for improving student listening before an important lesson: a brief 'stand and stretch' routine, and a return to seats with an emphasis on good posture. The stretching sequence has students stand, step back from their desks, and perform a short series of stretches to refresh energy and blood flow. Immediately afterward, students sit up straight with feet flat on the floor, which Linsin argues enhances alertness, breathing, and oxygen delivery to the brain, and grooves a habit of respect toward the speaker. He frames listening as a teachable skill rather than an innate trait, urging teachers to actively cultivate it through simple physical routines rather than accepting inattentiveness as unavoidable.
points: Two paired strategies are proposed to boost listening before an important lesson: a brief stand-and-stretch routine followed by a posture reset.
The stretch sequence involves standing, stepping back from desks, and reaching in several directions to refresh blood flow and energy.
Following the stretch, students sit with straight posture and feet flat on the floor, which is argued to enhance alertness and oxygen delivery to the brain.
Good posture is also framed as a habit that signals and reinforces respect for the speaker.
Listening is explicitly framed as a skill to be taught and cultivated through deliberate strategies, not an innate trait some students simply lack.
quotes: Listening is a topic we return to again and again here at SCM. Because it’s that important.
The idea is to get the blood flowing, to clear the cobwebs, and to refresh depleted energy stores, which any short spurt of exercise will do.
Now, it may feel old fashioned to do this, especially given the importance of allowing for individual differences in learning. But all students listen better when practicing good posture.
It will keep your students alert and energized. It will enhance breathing and oxygen delivery to the brain and groove a success habit that shows respect for the speaker.
Listening is a skill you teach and a habit you cultivate through your words and actions. It can be improved, often drastically, with simple strategies like the tandem above.
But you must act rather than bemoan. You must teach rather than accept.
